studies.title: Symptom dimensions are associated with reward processing in unmedicated persons at risk for psychosis.
studies.abstract: There is growing evidence that reward processing is disturbed in schizophrenia. However, it is uncertain whether this dysfunction predates or is secondary to the onset of psychosis. Studying 21 unmedicated persons at risk for psychosis plus 24 healthy controls (HCs) we used a incentive delay paradigm with monetary rewards during functional magnetic resonance imaging. During processing of reward information, at-risk individuals performed similarly well to controls and recruited the same brain areas. However, while anticipating rewards, the high-risk sample exhibited additional activation in the posterior cingulate cortex, and the medio- and superior frontal gyrus, whereas no significant group differences were found after rewards were administered. Importantly, symptom dimensions were differentially associated with anticipation and outcome of the reward. Positive symptoms were correlated with the anticipation signal in the ventral striatum (VS) and the right anterior insula (rAI). Negative symptoms were inversely linked to outcome-related signal within the VS, and depressive symptoms to outcome-related signal within the medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC). Our findings provide evidence for a reward-associated dysregulation that can be compensated by recruitment of additional prefrontal areas. We propose that stronger activations within VS and rAI when anticipating a reward reflect abnormal processing of potential future rewards. Moreover, according to the aberrant salience theory of psychosis, this may predispose a person to positive symptoms. Additionally, we report evidence that negative and depressive symptoms are differentially associated with the receipt of a reward, which might demonstrate a broader vulnerability to motivational and affective symptoms in persons at-risk for psychosis.

studies.title: Neurofunctional Reward Processing Changes in Cocaine Dependence During Recovery.
studies.abstract: Although reward processing appears altered in addiction, few studies track neurofunctional changes following treatment or relate these to measures of reduced drug use. The current study examined neurofunctional alterations in reward processing in cocaine dependence (CD) pretreatment and posttreatment to determine whether these changes relate to clinically meaningful outcome indicators. Treatment-seeking CD outpatients (N=29) underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging while performing a monetary incentive delay task (MIDT) pretreatment and posttreatment. The MIDT parses anticipatory from outcome phases of reward/loss processing. Abstinence indicators (negative urines, days abstinent from cocaine during follow-up) were collected throughout treatment and up to 1 year later. Healthy control (HC) participants (N=28) were also scanned twice with the MIDT. Relative to pretreatment, at posttreatment CD participants demonstrated increased anticipatory reward activity in the midbrain, thalamus, and precuneus (pFWE<0.05). Increased midbrain activity correlated with cocaine abstinence during the 1-year follow-up. Ventral striatal (VS) activity during loss anticipation correlated negatively with negative urine screens. HC group test-retest results showed decreased ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity during winning outcomes. CD-HC group-by-time differences revealed increased left inferior frontal gyrus activity in the CD group during anticipatory phases at posttreatment. In CD participants, increased posttreatment activity in dopamine-innervated regions suggests lowered thresholds in anticipatory signaling for non-drug rewards. Midbrain and VS responses may represent biomarkers associated with CD abstinence. Abstinence-related neurobiological changes occur in similar regions implicated during active use and may possibly be used to track progress during short- and long-term recovery.

studies.title: A functional endophenotype for sexual orientation in humans.
studies.abstract: Sexually arousing visual stimuli activate the human reward system and trigger sexual behavior. Here we performed event-related fMRI during visual processing of sexual core stimuli to pinpoint a neuronal correlate of sexual preference in humans. To dissociate gender of the stimulus from sexual preference, we studied male and female heterosexual and homosexual volunteers while they viewed sexual and nonsexual control stimuli. In contrast to previous work, we used core single-sex stimuli displaying male and female sexually aroused genitals. Since stimuli lacked any additional contextual information, they evoked no activity related to neuronal processing of faces, gestures or social interactions. Our prediction was that the sexual preference of the observer determines the neuronal responsiveness to pure male or female sexual stimuli in the human reward and motor system. Consistent with our prediction, the ventral striatum and the centromedian thalamus, showed a stronger neuronal response to preferred relative to non-preferred stimuli. Likewise, the ventral premotor cortex which is a key structure for imitative (mirror neurons) and tool-related (canonical neurons) actions showed a bilateral sexual preference-specific activation, suggesting that viewing sexually aroused genitals of the preferred sex triggers action representations of sexual behavior. The neuronal response of the ventral striatum, centromedian thalamus and ventral premotor cortex to preferred sexual stimuli was consistent across all groups. We propose that this invariant response pattern in core regions of the human reward and motor system represents a functional endophenotype for sexual orientation independent of the gender of the observer and gender of the stimulus.

studies.title: Neural correlates of the energetic value of food during visual processing and response inhibition.
studies.abstract: Previous research showed that human brain regions involved in reward and cognitive control are responsive to visually presented food stimuli, in particular high-energy foods. However, it is still to be determined whether the preference towards high-energy foods depends on their higher energy density (kcal/gram), or is based on the difference in energy content of the food items (total amount of kcal). Here we report the results of an fMRI study in which normal-weight healthy participants processed food images during a one-back task or were required to inhibit their response towards food stimuli during a Go/No-Go task. High-energy density (HD) and low-energy density (LD) foods were matched for energy content displayed. Food-related kitchen objects (OBJ) were used as control stimuli. The lateral occipital complex and the orbitofrontal cortex showed consistent higher activity in response to HD than LD foods, both during visual processing and response inhibition. This result suggests that images of HD foods, even when the amount of food shown is not associated with a higher energy content, elicit preferential visual processing - possibly involving attentional processes - and trigger a response from the reward system. We conclude that the human brain is able to distinguish food energy densities of food items during both active visual processing and response inhibition.

studies.title: Neural mechanisms underlying food motivation in children and adolescents.
studies.abstract: Dramatic increases in childhood obesity necessitate a more complete understanding of neural mechanisms of hunger and satiation in pediatric populations. In this study, normal weight children and adolescents underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanning before and after eating a meal. Participants showed increased activation to visual food stimuli in the amygdala, medial frontal/orbitofrontal cortex, and insula in the pre-meal condition; no regions of interest responded in the post-meal condition. These results closely parallel previous findings in adults. In addition, we found evidence for habituation to food stimuli in the amygdala within the pre-meal session. These findings provide evidence that normal patterns of neural activity related to food motivation begin in childhood. Results have implications for obese children and adults, who may have abnormal hunger and satiation mechanisms.

studies.title: The novelty exploration bonus and its attentional modulation.
studies.abstract: We hypothesized that novel stimuli represent salient learning signals that can motivate 'exploration' in search for potential rewards. In computational theories of reinforcement learning, this is referred to as the novelty 'exploration bonus' for rewards. If true, stimulus novelty should enhance the reward anticipation signals in brain areas that are part of dopaminergic circuitry and thereby reduce responses to reward outcomes. We investigated this hypothesis in two fMRI experiments. Images of complex natural scenes predicted monetary reward or a neutral outcome by virtue of depicting either indoor or outdoor scenes. Half of the reward-predicting and neutral images had been familiarized the day before, the other half were novel. In experiment 1, subjects indicated whether images were novel or familiar, whereas in experiment 2, they explicitly decided whether or not images predicted reward by depicting indoor or outdoor scenes. Novelty led to the hypothesized enhancement of mesolimbic reward prediction responses and concomitant reduction of mesolimbic responses to reward outcomes. However, this effect was strongly task-dependent and occurred only in experiment 2, when the reward-predicting property of each image was attended. Recognition memory for the novel and familiar stimuli (after 24h) was enhanced by reward anticipation in both tasks. These findings are compatible with the proposition that novelty can act as a bonus for rewards under conditions when rewards are explicitly attended, thus biasing the organism towards reward anticipation and providing a motivational signal for exploration.

studies.title: Associations between neural correlates of visual stimulus processing and set-shifting in ill and recovered women with anorexia nervosa.
studies.abstract: Women ill with anorexia nervosa (AN) have been shown to exhibit altered cognitive functioning, particularly poor set-shifting (SS). In this study, we investigated whether brain activation in frontal and parietal regions during visual stimulus processing correlates with SS ability. Women currently ill with AN (AN; N=14), recovered women (REC; N=14) and healthy controls (HC; N=15), viewed alternating blocks of food and non-food pictures during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The Berg's Card Sorting Task was completed outside the scanner to measure SS. A priori regions of interest (ROIs) were defined in frontal and parietal regions. The activation during visual stimulus processing in several ROIs correlated positively with poor SS ability in REC, particularly in the left dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC). The correlations with poor SS ability were opposite in AN patients, particularly in the right dACC. These findings underscore that addressing heightened levels of cognitive control associated with higher frontal activation could reduce cognitive inflexibility in recovered women. In AN, greater activation in frontal and parietal regions might be necessary to perform at normal levels during various tasks. Thus, weight restoration could be necessary for AN patients prior to addressing cognitive inflexibility.

studies.title: Functional MRI of Challenging Food Choices: Forced Choice between Equally Liked High- and Low-Calorie Foods in the Absence of Hunger.
studies.abstract: We are continuously exposed to food and during the day we make many food choices. These choices play an important role in the regulation of food intake and thereby in weight management. Therefore, it is important to obtain more insight into the mechanisms that underlie these choices. While several food choice functional MRI (fMRI) studies have been conducted, the effect of energy content on neural responses during food choice has, to our knowledge, not been investigated before. Our objective was to examine brain responses during food choices between equally liked high- and low-calorie foods in the absence of hunger. During a 10-min fMRI scan 19 normal weight volunteers performed a forced-choice task. Food pairs were matched on individual liking but differed in perceived and actual caloric content (high-low). Food choice compared with non-food choice elicited stronger unilateral activation in the left insula, superior temporal sulcus, posterior cingulate gyrus and (pre)cuneus. This suggests that the food stimuli were more salient despite subject's low motivation to eat. The right superior temporal sulcus (STS) was the only region that exhibited greater activation for high versus low calorie food choices between foods matched on liking. Together with previous studies, this suggests that STS activation during food evaluation and choice may reflect the food's biological relevance independent of food preference. This novel finding warrants further research into the effects of hunger state and weight status on STS, which may provide a marker of biological relevance.

studies.title: Brain processing of visual stimuli representing sexual penetration versus core and animal-reminder disgust in women with lifelong vaginismus.
studies.abstract: It has been proposed that disgust evolved to protect humans from contamination. Through eliciting the overwhelming urge to withdraw from the disgusting stimuli, it would facilitate avoidance of contact with pathogens. The physical proximity implied in sexual intercourse provides ample opportunity for contamination and may thus set the stage for eliciting pathogen disgust. Building on this, it has been argued that the involuntary muscle contraction characteristic of vaginismus (i.e., inability to have vaginal penetration) may be elicited by the prospect of penetration by potential contaminants. To further investigate this disgust-based interpretation of vaginismus (in DSM-5 classified as a Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder, GPPPD) we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine if women with vaginismus (n = 21) show relatively strong convergence in their brain responses towards sexual penetration- and disgust-related pictures compared to sexually asymptomatic women (n = 21) and women suffering from vulvar pain (dyspareunia/also classified as GPPPD in the DSM-5, n = 21). At the subjective level, both clinical groups rated penetration stimuli as more disgusting than asymptomatic women. However, the brain responses to penetration stimuli did not differ between groups. In addition, there was considerable conjoint brain activity in response to penetration and disgust pictures, which yield for both animal-reminder (e.g., mutilation) and core (e.g., rotten food) disgust domains. However, this overlap in brain activation was similar for all groups. A possible explanation for the lack of vaginismus-specific brain responses lies in the alleged female ambiguity (procreation/pleasure vs. contamination/disgust) toward penetration: generally in women a (default) disgust response tendency may prevail in the absence of sexual readiness. Accordingly, a critical next step would be to examine the processing of penetration stimuli following the induction of sexual arousal.

studies.title: Neural processing of food and emotional stimuli in adolescent and adult anorexia nervosa patients.
studies.abstract: A constant preoccupation with food and restrictive eating are main symptoms of anorexia nervosa (AN). Imaging studies revealed aberrant neural activation patterns in brain regions processing hedonic and reward reactions as well as-potentially aversive-emotions. An imbalance between so called "bottom-up" and "top-down" control areas is discussed. The present study is focusing on neural processing of disease-specific food stimuli and emotional stimuli and its developmental course in adolescent and adult AN patients and could offer new insight into differential mechanisms underlying shorter or more chronic disease.

studies.title: Cortical and limbic activation during viewing of high- versus low-calorie foods.
studies.abstract: Despite the high prevalence of obesity, eating disorders, and weight-related health problems in modernized cultures, the neural systems regulating human feeding remain poorly understood. Therefore, we applied functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study the cerebral responses of 13 healthy normal-weight adult women as they viewed color photographs of food. The motivational salience of the stimuli was manipulated by presenting images from three categories: high-calorie foods, low-calorie foods, and nonedible dining-related utensils. Both food categories were associated with bilateral activation of the amygdala and ventromedial prefrontal cortex. High-calorie foods yielded significant activation within the medial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, corpus callosum, and cerebellum. Low-calorie foods yielded smaller regions of focal activation within medial orbitofrontal cortex; primary gustatory/somatosensory cortex; and superior, middle, and medial temporal regions. Findings suggest that the amygdala may be responsive to a general category of biologically relevant stimuli such as food, whereas separate ventromedial prefrontal systems may be activated depending on the perceived reward value or motivational salience of food stimuli.

studies.title: Changes in alcohol-related brain networks across the first year of college: a prospective pilot study using fMRI effective connectivity mapping.
studies.abstract: The upsurge in alcohol use that often occurs during the first year of college has been convincingly linked to a number of negative psychosocial consequences and may negatively affect brain development. In this longitudinal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) pilot study, we examined changes in neural responses to alcohol cues across the first year of college in a normative sample of late adolescents. Participants (N=11) were scanned three times across their first year of college (summer, first semester, second semester), while completing a go/no-go task in which images of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages were the response cues. A state-of-the-art effective connectivity mapping technique was used to capture spatiotemporal relations among brain regions of interest (ROIs) at the level of the group and the individual. Effective connections among ROIs implicated in cognitive control were greatest at the second assessment (when negative consequences of alcohol use increased), and effective connections among ROIs implicated in emotion processing were lower (and response times were slower) when participants were instructed to respond to alcohol cues compared to non-alcohol cues. These preliminary findings demonstrate the value of a prospective effective connectivity approach for understanding adolescent changes in alcohol-related neural processes.

studies.title: Neural Substrates of Sexual Desire in Individuals with Problematic Hypersexual Behavior.
studies.abstract: Studies on the characteristics of individuals with hypersexual disorder have been accumulating due to increasing concerns about problematic hypersexual behavior (PHB). Currently, relatively little is known about the underlying behavioral and neural mechanisms of sexual desire. Our study aimed to investigate the neural correlates of sexual desire with event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Twenty-three individuals with PHB and 22 age-matched healthy controls were scanned while they passively viewed sexual and nonsexual stimuli. The subjects' levels of sexual desire were assessed in response to each sexual stimulus. Relative to controls, individuals with PHB experienced more frequent and enhanced sexual desire during exposure to sexual stimuli. Greater activation was observed in the caudate nucleus, inferior parietal lobe, dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus, thalamus, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in the PHB group than in the control group. In addition, the hemodynamic patterns in the activated areas differed between the groups. Consistent with the findings of brain imaging studies of substance and behavior addiction, individuals with the behavioral characteristics of PHB and enhanced desire exhibited altered activation in the prefrontal cortex and subcortical regions. In conclusion, our results will help to characterize the behaviors and associated neural mechanisms of individuals with PHB.

studies.title: Neural correlates of behavioral preference for culturally familiar drinks.
studies.abstract: Coca-Cola (Coke) and Pepsi are nearly identical in chemical composition, yet humans routinely display strong subjective preferences for one or the other. This simple observation raises the important question of how cultural messages combine with content to shape our perceptions; even to the point of modifying behavioral preferences for a primary reward like a sugared drink. We delivered Coke and Pepsi to human subjects in behavioral taste tests and also in passive experiments carried out during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Two conditions were examined: (1) anonymous delivery of Coke and Pepsi and (2) brand-cued delivery of Coke and Pepsi. For the anonymous task, we report a consistent neural response in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex that correlated with subjects' behavioral preferences for these beverages. In the brand-cued experiment, brand knowledge for one of the drinks had a dramatic influence on expressed behavioral preferences and on the measured brain responses.

studies.title: Neural responsivity to food cues in fasted and fed states pre and post gastric bypass surgery.
studies.abstract: Reductions in mesolimbic responsivity have been noted following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB; Ochner et al., 2011a). Given potential for postoperative increases in postprandial gut (satiety) peptides to affect mesolimbic neural responsivity, we hypothesized that: (1) post RYGB changes in mesolimbic responsivity would be greater in the fed relative to the fasted state and; (2) fasted vs. fed state differences in mesolimbic responsivity would be greater post-relative to pre-surgery. fMRI was used to asses neural responsivity to high- and low-calorie food cues in five women 1 mo pre- and 1 mo post-RYGB. Scans were repeated in fasted and fed states. Significant post RYGB decreases in the insula, ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) responsivity were found in the fasted state. These changes were larger than neural changes in the fed state, which were non-significant. Preoperatively, fasted vs. fed differences in neural responsivity were greater in the precuneus, with large but nonsignificant clusters in the vmPFC and dlPFC. Postoperatively, however, no fasted vs. fed differences in neural responsivity were noted. Results were opposite to that predicted and appear inconsistent with the initial hypothesis that postoperative increases in postprandial gut peptides are the primary driver of postoperative changes in neural responsivity.

studies.title: Accelerated HF-rTMS Protocol has a Rate-Dependent Effect on dACC Activation in Alcohol-Dependent Patients: An Open-Label Feasibility Study.
studies.abstract: The application of accelerated high-frequency (HF) repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) could be a potential treatment option for alcohol-dependent patients and may result in a faster clinical response. In this open-label HF-rTMS feasibility study, we wanted to replicate previous findings of baseline brain activation as a predictor of relapse, and to evaluate how this intervention influences the relapse neurocircuit of "treatment-seeking" alcohol-dependent patients, by means of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) cue-exposure paradigms. Because relapsing patients have a diminished resilience of the emotion regulation/cognitive control system, before HF-rTMS treatment, we expected lower neuronal activation of especially the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) during the presentation of alcohol-related cues in these patients. The relapse neurocircuit should be modified after accelerated HF-rTMS treatment, only in those patients who did not relapse.

studies.title: Distinct and overlapping fusiform activation to faces and food.
studies.abstract: The fusiform cortex is a part of the ventral visual stream and is typically associated with face processing. Indeed, a subregion of the fusiform has been named the "fusiform face area" or FFA, based on its robust response to faces relative to other objects. In a separate literature, appetizing food has also been shown to activate bilateral fusiform cortex, yet no study to date has directly compared face and food responses within the same paradigm. Here, we use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to compare face and food responses in ventral visual cortex and other regions that are typically associated with face processing. We present evidence that a region of the left fusiform cortex (typically associated with face processing) actually responds equally to faces and food. We go on to describe the similarities and differences in location of face- and food-responses in the fusiform, the relationship of fusiform activation to body mass index (BMI), and resting state connectivity of face- and food-selective fusiform. Results are interpreted within a model in which motivational relevance or value influence fusiform response.

studies.title: Effects of cognitive bias modification training on neural signatures of alcohol approach tendencies in male alcohol-dependent patients.
studies.abstract: Alcohol-dependent patients have been shown to faster approach than avoid alcohol stimuli on the Approach Avoidance Task (AAT). This so-called alcohol approach bias has been associated with increased brain activation in the medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens. Cognitive bias modification (CBM) has been used to retrain the approach bias with the clinically relevant effect of decreasing relapse rates one year later. The effects of CBM on neural signatures of approach/avoidance tendencies remain hitherto unknown. In a double-blind placebo-controlled design, 26 alcohol-dependent in-patients were assigned to a CBM or a placebo training group. Both groups performed the AAT for three weeks: in CBM training, patients pushed away 90 percent of alcohol cues; this rate was 50 percent in placebo training. Before and after training, patients performed the AAT offline, and in a 3 T magnetic resonance imaging scanner. The relevant neuroimaging contrast for the alcohol approach bias was the difference between approaching versus avoiding alcohol cues relative to soft drink cues: [(alcohol pull > alcohol push)  > (soft drink pull > soft drink push)]. Before training, both groups showed significant alcohol approach bias-related activation in the medial prefrontal cortex. After training, patients in the CBM group showed stronger reductions in medial prefrontal cortex activation compared with the placebo group. Moreover, these reductions correlated with reductions in approach bias scores in the CBM group only. This suggests that CBM affects neural mechanisms involved in the automatic alcohol approach bias, which may be important for the clinical effectiveness of CBM.

studies.title: Functional insights into aberrant brain responses and integration in patients with lifelong premature ejaculation.
studies.abstract: Even though lifelong premature ejaculation (PE) is highly prevalent, few studies have investigated the neural mechanisms underlying PE. The extent and pattern of brain activation can be determined through a version of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with erotic picture stimuli (task fMRI) and a resting-state fMRI (rs fMRI). We showed that the brain activity in the left inferior frontal gyrus and left insula was decreased both during the task and in the resting state, while there was higher activation in the right middle temporal gyrus during the task. Higher functional connectivity was found in PE between those three brain areas and the bilateral middle cingulate cortex, right middle frontal gyrus and supplementary motor area. Moreover, the brain activity had positive correlation with clinical rating scales, such as intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) and the Chinese Index of Premature Ejaculation (CIPE). These findings revealed that brain responses and functional integration in certain brain areas are impaired in cases of PE, which was consistently supported by multiple measurements obtained using a task and rs fMRI approach.

studies.title: Neural correlates of top-down guidance of attention to food: An fMRI study.
studies.abstract: We investigated the neural correlates of working memory guided attentional selection of food versus non-food stimuli in young women. Participants were thirty-two women, aged 20.6y (± 0.5) who were presented with a cue (food or non-food item) to hold in working memory. Subsequently, they had to search for a target in a 2-item display where target and distractor stimuli were each flanked by a picture of a food or a non-food item. The behavioural data showed that attention is particularly efficiently drawn to food stimuli when thinking about food. Using fMRI, we found that holding a non-food versus food stimulus in working memory was associated with increased activity in occipital gyrus, fusiform, inferior and superior frontal gyrus. In the posterior cingulum, retrosplenial cortex, a food item that re-appeared in the search array when it was held in memory led to a reduced response, compared to when it did not re-appear. The reverse effect was found for non-food stimuli. The extent of the reappearance effect correlated with the attentional capture of food as measured behaviourally. In conclusion, these results suggest that holding food in mind may bias attention because thinking of food facilitated neuronal responses to sensory input related to food stimuli and because holding food-related information in mind is less taxing on memory.

studies.title: High field FMRI reveals thalamocortical integration of segregated cognitive and emotional processing in mediodorsal and intralaminar thalamic nuclei.
studies.abstract: Thalamocortical loops, connecting functionally segregated, higher order cortical regions, and basal ganglia, have been proposed not only for well described motor and sensory regions, but also for limbic and prefrontal areas relevant for affective and cognitive processes. These functions are, however, more specific to humans, rendering most invasive neuroanatomical approaches impossible and interspecies translations difficult. In contrast, non-invasive imaging of functional neuroanatomy using fMRI allows for the development of elaborate task paradigms capable of testing the specific functionalities proposed for these circuits. Until recently, spatial resolution largely limited the anatomical definition of functional clusters at the level of distinct thalamic nuclei. Since their anatomical distinction seems crucial not only for the segregation of cognitive and limbic loops but also for the detection of their functional interaction during cognitive-emotional integration, we applied high resolution fMRI on 7 Tesla. Using an event-related design, we could isolate thalamic effects for preceding attention as well as experience of erotic stimuli. We could demonstrate specific thalamic effects of general emotional arousal in mediodorsal nucleus and effects specific to preceding attention and expectancy in intralaminar centromedian/parafascicular complex. These thalamic effects were paralleled by specific coactivations in the head of caudate nucleus as well as segregated portions of rostral or caudal cingulate cortex and anterior insula supporting distinct thalamo-striato-cortical loops. In addition to predescribed effects of sexual arousal in hypothalamus and ventral striatum, high resolution fMRI could extent this network to paraventricular thalamus encompassing laterodorsal and parataenial nuclei. We could lend evidence to segregated subcortical loops which integrate cognitive and emotional aspects of basic human behavior such as sexual processing.

studies.title: Impaired inhibitory control in anorexia nervosa elicited by physical activity stimuli.
studies.abstract: Besides food restriction, hyperactivity is considered a key behavioral trait of anorexia nervosa (AN), playing a major role in the pathogenesis and progression of the disorder. However, the underlying neurophysiology remains poorly understood. We used functional magnetic resonance imaging during two affective go/no-go tasks to probe inhibitory control in response to stimuli depicting physical activity vs inactivity and food vs non-food in AN patients compared with 26 healthy athlete and non-athlete controls. We hypothesized that neural correlates of behavioral inhibition are biased by the emotional information of the stimuli in AN patients, leading to a differential neural inhibitory pattern during the two tasks. Indeed, we found reduced response inhibition for food and non-food images in the putamen, while stimuli depicting physical activity resulted in an exaggerated response of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and cerebellum in AN patients. However, both AN patients and athletes revealed an increased response in the somatosensory cortex to physical activity stimuli. These results suggest that physical activity stimuli might place an increased demand on the inhibitory control system in AN patients. The resulting hyperactivity of the PFC and cerebellum may lead to altered executive function and motor control, sustaining increased physical activity in AN patients.

studies.title: Functional imaging in obese children responding to long-term sports therapy.
studies.abstract: Functional imaging studies on responders and non-responders to therapeutic interventions in obese children are rare. We applied fMRI before and after a one-year sports therapy in 14 obese or overweight children aged 7-16 years. During scanning, participants observed a set of standardized pictures from food categories, sports, and pleasant and neutral images. We were interested in alterations of the cerebral activation to food images in association with changes in the BMI-standard deviation score (BMI-SDS) after therapy and therefore separated the observation group into two outcome subgroups. One with reduction of BMI-SDS >0.2 (responder group) and one without (non-responder group). Before therapy fMRI-activation between groups did not differ. After therapy we found the following results: in response to food images, obese children of the responder group showed increased activation in the left putamen when compared with the non-responder group. Pleasant images evoked increased insula activation in the responder group. Only the responder group showed enhanced activity within areas known to store trained motor patterns in response to sports images. Both the putamen and the insula are involved in the processing of emotional valence and were only active for the therapy responders during the observation of food or pleasant stimuli. Elevated activity in these regions might possibly be seen in the context of an increase of dopaminergic response to emotional positive stimuli during intervention. In addition, sport images activated motor representations only in those subjects who profited from the sports therapy. Overall, an altered response to rewarding and pleasant images and an increased recruitment of motor engrams during observations of sports pictures indicates a more normal cerebral processing in response to these stimuli after successful sports therapy in obese children.

studies.title: Reward, addiction, and emotion regulation systems associated with rejection in love.
studies.abstract: Romantic rejection causes a profound sense of loss and negative affect. It can induce clinical depression and in extreme cases lead to suicide and/or homicide. To begin to identify the neural systems associated with this natural loss state, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to study 10 women and 5 men who had recently been rejected by a partner but reported they were still intensely "in love." Participants alternately viewed a photograph of their rejecting beloved and a photograph of a familiar, individual, interspersed with a distraction-attention task. Their responses while looking at their rejecter included love, despair, good, and bad memories, and wondering why this happened. Activation specific to the image of the beloved occurred in areas associated with gains and losses, craving and emotion regulation and included the ventral tegmental area (VTA) bilaterally, ventral striatum, medial and lateral orbitofrontal/prefrontal cortex, and cingulate gyrus. Compared with data from happily-in-love individuals, the regional VTA activation suggests that mesolimbic reward/survival systems are involved in romantic passion regardless of whether one is happily or unhappily in love. Forebrain activations associated with motivational relevance, gain/loss, cocaine craving, addiction, and emotion regulation suggest that higher-order systems subject to experience and learning also may mediate the rejection reaction. The results show activation of reward systems, previously identified by monetary stimuli, in a natural, endogenous, negative emotion state. Activation of areas involved in cocaine addiction may help explain the obsessive behaviors associated with rejection in love.

studies.title: Neural predictors of giving in to temptation in daily life.
studies.abstract: The ability to control desires, whether for food, sex, or drugs, enables people to function successfully within society. Yet, in tempting situations, strong impulses often result in self-control failure. Although many triggers of self-control failure have been identified, the question remains as to why some individuals are more likely than others to give in to temptation. In this study, we combined functional neuroimaging and experience sampling to determine if there are brain markers that predict whether people act on their food desires in daily life. We examined food-cue-related activity in the nucleus accumbens (NAcc), as well as activity associated with response inhibition in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG). Greater NAcc activity was associated with greater likelihood of self-control failures, whereas IFG activity supported successful resistance to temptations. These findings demonstrate an important role for the neural mechanisms underlying desire and self-control in people's real-world experiences of temptations.

studies.title: A Neglected Topic in Neuroscience: Replicability of fMRI Results With Specific Reference to ANOREXIA NERVOSA.
studies.abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies report impaired functional correlates of cognition and emotion in mental disorders. The validity of preexisting studies needs to be confirmed through replication studies, which there is a lack of. So far, most replication studies have been conducted on non-patients (NP) and primarily investigated cognitive and motor tasks. To fill this gap, we conducted the first fMRI replication study to investigate brain function using disease-related food stimuli in patients with anorexia nervosa (AN). Using fMRI, we investigated 31 AN patients and 27 NP for increased amygdala and reduced midcingulate activation when viewing food and non-food stimuli, as reported by the original study (11AN, 11NP; Joos et al., 2011). Similar to the previous study, we observed in the within group comparisons (food>non-food) a frontoinsular activation for both groups. Although in AN the recorded activation clustered more prominently and extended into the cingulate cortex. In the between-group comparisons, the increased amygdala and reduced midcingulate activation could not be replicated. Instead, AN showed a higher activation of the cingulate cortices, the pre-/postcentral gyrus and the inferior parietal lobe. Unlike in the initial study, no significant differences between NP>AN could be observed. The inconsistency of results and the non-replication of the study could have several reasons, such as high inter-individual variance of functional correlates of emotion processing, as well as intra-individual variances and the smaller group size of the initial study. These results underline the importance of replication for assessing the reliability and validity of results from fMRI research.

Inclusion criteria met: I4 (within-participant contrasts: drug-cue vs neutral were reported), I5 (whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results with family-wise error correction), I6 (voxelwise results reported in main text/figures/supplement), and I7 (participant age/sex and methodological details reported). Exclusion criteria met: none (E3–E6 do not apply). Full text appears complete and contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore the paper must be excluded from a meta-analysis restricted to visual cue-reactivity studies.

This is an empirical fMRI study that used visual heroin-related cues (images) in a cue-reactivity task and reports within-participant contrasts (heroin-related images > neutral images). Group-level voxelwise task-evoked statistical results are reported (random-effects GLM, FDR-corrected whole-brain results, p<0.01, cluster extent threshold), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain voxelwise evidence. The paper provides participant demographics (male, ages reported), MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5). Full article text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria relevant to the meta-analysis are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI cue-reactivity study in opioid use disorder using visual stimuli (heroin or prescription-opioid images vs neutral and other categories). The paper reports within-participant contrasts (drug > neutral) at the individual and group levels, ROI analyses, and, crucially, exploratory whole-brain voxelwise regression analyses (TFCE-corrected) with reported cluster coordinates (Table 2) and figures. MRI field strength (3T), preprocessing (SPM12, MATLAB) and participant demographics (age, sex) and cue types are reported. Therefore it meets all required inclusion criteria for task-evoked voxelwise results and necessary methodological details. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study of smoking cue-reactivity using visual stimuli. The study presents smoking-related versus neutral visual cues and reports within-participant contrasts (smoking>neutral) and group-level voxelwise analyses (three-way ANOVA) with reported peak coordinates and SPM maps. MRI field strength (3.0 T) and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5) are reported, participant characteristics (male smokers, ages summarized) and cue types are described. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only contrasts, or non-empirical paper) apply. Full article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and should be included in the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI cue-reactivity study using visual alcohol images (alcohol vs neutral) in recently detoxified alcohol-dependent patients, meeting the meta-analysis scope. It includes a within-participant contrast (alcohol > neutral) and reports group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses with multiple-comparison correction (AlphaSim cluster-wise FWE) and cluster coordinates/tables/figures. They also report an ROI (ventral striatum) small-volume analysis, but whole-brain voxelwise results are present and qualifying. Key methodological details (3T MRI, SPM preprocessing, participant age/sex, cue type) are reported. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-state only, and includes the required within-participant contrast). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study should be INCLUDED.

This is an empirical fMRI study in human smokers that includes visual cues (picture indicating puff, money, or neutral) during a rewarded-guessing task, satisfying the visual cue requirement. It reports within-participant contrasts of puff > neutral (drug cue > control) and money > neutral, with group-level voxelwise analyses conducted within a priori anatomical ROI mask (striatum and mPFC) using cluster-size correction within that mask (i.e., small-volume-corrected results). Whole-brain exploratory results are also reported. Participant demographics, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM8) are provided. Thus inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 are met. No exclusion criteria are met. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical 3T fMRI study of smoking cue reactivity that includes clear visual stimuli (grayscaled images) alongside haptic conditions. The study reports within-participant contrasts (e.g., VS–VC, HS–HC) and group-level, whole-brain RFX-GLM/ANOVA results with cluster-level multiple-comparison correction and coordinates/tables. Participant demographics, cue types, MRI field strength, and preprocessing/statistical software are reported. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7; no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, references).

This study is an empirical fMRI investigation of smoking cue reactivity using visual stimuli in adolescent smokers. It reports within-participant contrasts of smoking cues > neutral cues, presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise results (significant activations reported at p<.001 with cluster threshold) and a-priori ROI analyses, and provides participant demographics, cue types, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5). The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. No exclusion criteria are met. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and should be included.

This is an fMRI study of alcohol (drug) cue-reactivity using visual picture stimuli and includes within-participant contrasts of alcohol-associated versus control stimuli. Group-level voxelwise task-evoked statistical results are reported (SPM99, threshold p<0.001 uncorrected, cluster-size reported) with tables/figures of regional activations. Participant demographics (age, sex), cue type, MRI field strength (1.5 T), and preprocessing/statistical software are reported. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7, and does not violate any exclusion criteria (no ROI-only or connectivity-only reporting, and includes qualifying within-participant contrasts).

This is an empirical fMRI study of alcohol (drug-related) cue-reactivity that used visual picture cues (and a taste) and reported within-subject voxelwise contrasts (alcohol > beverage; alcohol > visual control). Group-level random-effects SPM2 analyses are reported (thresholded maps, tables/figures with peak coordinates), and a small-volume ROI analysis of the ventral striatum is also presented. MRI field strength (1.5T), preprocessing and SPM2 software, and participant demographics are described. The full article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-subject cue>control contrasts). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and is eligible for inclusion in the meta-analysis of visual cue-reactivity fMRI studies.

This is an fMRI study of cigarette cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (ISIS smoking images vs IAPS neutral images) with a within-subject contrast (appetitive smoking-related > neutral). Group-level voxelwise task-evoked results are reported via small-volume-corrected ROI analyses (SVC, p<0.05 FDR) and coordinates/figures are provided. Participant age/sex, cue type, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5) are reported. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI cue-reactivity study that includes a clear visual cue component (45 s cigarette video cues) and computes within-participant contrasts (Cigarette Cues > Control Cues; Alcohol Cues > Control Cues). Group-level voxelwise GLMs were run (38 whole-brain GLMs) to define precuneus peak voxels (coordinates reported), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain/small-volume-corrected task-evoked results; results are reported in text and with peak coordinates. Participant demographics, cue types, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (FSL) are reported. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-subject cue>control contrasts, and is original human fMRI data). Full text is complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion present). Thus the study meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis of fMRI cue-reactivity using visual stimuli.

This is an empirical fMRI study of smoking (drug) cue-reactivity using visual stimuli. The study reports within-subject Smoking>Neutral contrasts and conducts group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses (FLAME) with cluster-level correction (z=3.1, Pcorrected<.05), and presents results in tables/figures. Methods report participant age/sex, cue type (visual smoking and matched neutral images), MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (FSL). The full text includes introduction, detailed methods, results, and discussion, so the full text appears complete. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, contains within-participant cue>control contrasts, and is original human fMRI data). Therefore the study meets all required inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis of visual cue-reactivity.

This is an empirical fMRI study using visual cues (heroin-related images and IAPS pleasant/neutral images) in abstinent opioid-dependent males and controls. The paper includes within-participant contrasts (heroin vs. baseline; heroin vs. neutral; pleasant vs. baseline), reports group-level voxelwise task-evoked results with coordinates and corrected thresholds (FDR) and regression analyses (voxelwise), and provides scanner field strength (3T) and preprocessing/statistics (SPM2). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criterion applies.

This is an empirical task-fMRI study of smoking cue-reactivity that includes clear visual cues (unisensory visual pictures) and multimodal (visual+odor) conditions. It reports within-participant contrasts of smoking>neutral pictures (CIG-I vs NEU-I) under both odorless and cigarette-odor conditions. Whole-brain voxelwise group-level analyses are reported (cluster-thresholded Z>2.3, p<0.05 corrected), and ROI post-hoc analyses are also presented. Participant demographics, cue types, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (FSL/FEAT) are reported. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-subject cue>control contrasts, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore the study meets the review inclusion criteria and should be INCLUDED.

This is an empirical fMRI study of cannabis cue reactivity using visual cannabis vs neutral stimuli (blocked-design) with within-subject contrasts (cannabis > neutral). Group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses (ANOVA and voxelwise t tests) are reported with cluster-level FWE correction and region-of-interest follow-ups; results are presented in the main text and supplementary materials. Participant demographics and cue type are described. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical task-fMRI study using visual alcohol cues as distractors during a response-inhibition task (meets I3). It includes within-participant contrasts of alcohol > neutral/scramble (meets I4). Group-level voxelwise task-evoked statistical results are reported using voxel-wise p<0.001 with cluster-extent correction to achieve pFWE<0.05 and identified clusters/ROIs (meets I5 and I6). Methods report participant demographics (all-male sample, N and ages in tables), MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM8), satisfying I7. The study does not meet any exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and reports within-subject cue>control contrasts). Full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (fulltext_incomplete=false). Therefore this study should be INCLUDED for the meta-analysis of visual drug cue-reactivity.

This is an empirical fMRI study using visual film cues (cocaine, sex, nature) to evoke cue-induced craving in cocaine users. It includes within-participant contrasts (cocaine film vs nature film) and group-level voxelwise analyses (one-sample and two-sample t tests, voxel-wise threshold p=0.0025 with cluster extent), with results reported as activation clusters/tables and figures. The manuscript reports participant demographics (age/sex), cue types, MRI field strength (1.5 T), and preprocessing/statistical software (AFNI) and provides whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results. Full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical task-evoked fMRI study of alcohol cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (alcohol vs. neutral images). The paper reports within-participant contrasts (alcohol>neutral), group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses with explicit thresholding and cluster correction (AlphaSim/FWE) and reports regional activations (peaks/ROIs). MRI field strength (3T), preprocessing (SPM5/SPM8) and task details are provided. Therefore all inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so it appears complete.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using visual cues (videos of cocaine and food) and includes within-participant contrasts of cocaine>food. Group-level voxelwise task-evoked analyses are reported (whole-brain contrasts with cluster correction, thresholding and reported activations), satisfying requirements for voxelwise results. Reporting includes participant demographics (matched age/sex/education), MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (AFNI). Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not solely connectivity/resting-state, includes within-subject cue>control contrasts). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an fMRI study using visual cue videos (e-cigarette vs electronic toothbrush) and reports within-subject contrasts of salient (e-cigarette) > neutral videos. Group-level voxelwise analyses were conducted (random-effects GLM, repeated-measures ANOVA) with cluster-level multiple-comparison correction and reported cluster coordinates and regions, satisfying the requirement for whole-brain/small-volume-corrected task-evoked voxelwise results. MRI field strength (3 T), preprocessing/statistical software (BrainVoyager QX), cue type, and participant age range/sex information are reported. Full article contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so fulltext is complete. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, or non-empirical) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study using visual drug-related film cues in amphetamine-dependent patients. It reports a within-subject contrast Drug movies > Neutral movies with group-level voxelwise results (whole-brain FWE-corrected activations) and also reports ROI analyses; MRI field strength (3T), participant demographics (age, all male), cue type (films), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM12) are provided. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. All inclusion criteria I3–I7 are met and no exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical fMRI study of alcohol cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (alcohol vs neutral pictures) in within-subject block and event-related paradigms. The paper reports within-participant contrasts (alcohol > neutral) at the group level, with voxelwise whole-brain analyses and cluster-correction (AlphaSim), and provides MNI coordinates and figures/tables for significant clusters. Key methodological details are reported (participants’ age range and sex distribution, cue type, 3T MRI, preprocessing/statistics using SPM8). No exclusion criteria are met. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and qualifies for inclusion in the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical human fMRI study of alcohol cue-reactivity using visual picture cues (alcohol vs non-alcohol beverages). The paper reports within-participant contrasts (alcohol > beverage) and group-level voxelwise statistical analyses using SPM5 (thresholds and cluster extent reported) with MNI coordinates and figures/tables of activation (including ventral striatum). Imaging was acquired at 3.0T and methods/results/discussion are present in the full text. Thus it meets the meta-analysis scope and all required inclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of alcohol (drug) cue reactivity using visual stimuli (alcohol vs soft drink pictures). It includes within-subject contrasts of alcohol>soft drink (pretraining and pre-post), and reports group-level voxelwise task-evoked results with small-volume FWE-corrected findings in anatomically defined regions (amygdala; reported coordinates and p-values). MRI field strength (3T) and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM8) are reported. The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for visual cue fMRI cue-reactivity and provides qualifying voxelwise results.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using visual stimuli (smoking and food videos) with within-participant contrasts (Smoking>Food, Smoking>Baseline, Food>Baseline). Group-level voxelwise whole-brain results are reported with cluster correction and tables/figures. Participant demographics (age, sex), MRI field strength (3T), cue type, preprocessing (FSL tools), and statistical software are reported. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical fMRI study of alcohol (drug) cue-reactivity using visual alcohol-related pictures with within-participant contrasts (alcohol > neutral) at group level. The paper reports voxelwise whole-brain analyses (cluster threshold p<.001 uncorrected) and small-volume-corrected (FWE-SV) results in striatal regions, and provides participant demographics, cue type, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria and violates none.

This study used ASL fMRI with cocaine-related video cues (visual stimuli) but did not report a within-participant voxelwise task-evoked cue>control contrast. The analyses focused on seed-based functional connectivity (amygdala whole-brain regression) and wavelet transform coherence (WTC) of CBF time series, not on task-evoked activation maps (drug cues > control) at the group voxelwise level. Therefore it fails to meet the required within-subject cue>control contrast and qualifying task-evoked voxelwise result. Exclusion criteria applied: E4 (study reports seed-based connectivity/WTC without an accompanying qualifying task-evoked voxelwise result) and E5 (no within-participant cue>control contrast presented). Inclusion criteria satisfied: I3 (used visual cocaine-related video cues) and I7 (reported participant characteristics and MRI details). Inclusion criteria not met: I4 (no within-participant drug-cue > control contrast) and I5 (no group-level voxelwise task-evoked results reported). Full text appears complete.

This is an fMRI study of natural reward (food) cue-reactivity using visual stimuli. It uses a within-participant contrast of food pictures > low-level control pictures, reports group-level voxelwise task-evoked results across the whole brain (FDR-corrected and uncorrected thresholds) with tables and figures of coordinates, and provides participant demographics, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for visual cue-based reward reactivity and provides qualifying whole-brain voxelwise results suitable for meta-analysis.

This is an event-related fMRI study using visual smoking cues (photographs) and control images, meeting I3. The authors computed a within-participant smoking cue > control cue contrast and entered these contrast images into group-level random-effects voxelwise analyses (SPM2), with results reported as whole-brain voxelwise maps, tables of coordinates, and figures, satisfying I4, I5, and I6. The Methods report MRI field strength (1.5 T), preprocessing and statistical software (SPM2), and participant demographics (age/sex) and cue type, satisfying I7. The paper is empirical and provides whole-brain task-evoked voxelwise group results (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only), so no exclusion criteria (E3–E5) apply. Full article content (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) is present. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and should be INCLUDED in the meta-analysis.

This is an empirical fMRI study of alcohol-modulated smoking cue reactivity using visual cigarette-related images in heavy-drinking nondaily smokers. It includes within-subject contrasts of smoking vs control cues (reported in post hoc tests and ANOVA interactions) and reports group-level voxelwise task-evoked results using whole-brain analyses with FDR correction for ventral striatum as well as uncorrected whole-brain results; results are presented in figures/tables. Methods report participant age/sex, cue type, 3T MRI field strength, and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM2). The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7; no exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply.

This is an fMRI study of natural reward (food) cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (images of marzipan objects). It includes a within-participant contrast of CS+ > CS- (task-evoked cue>control) at the group level and reports voxelwise results: whole-brain exploratory clusters (p<.001 uncorrected) and small-volume-corrected (SVC) FWE-corrected group-level effects in the left caudate and right amygdala. Methods and sample details (age/sex, MRI field strength 3T, preprocessing with SPM12) are reported. Thus the study satisfies the meta-analysis inclusion criteria (visual cues, within-subject cue>control contrast, and at least one SVC/voxelwise group-level result) and does not meet any exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-subject contrast, empirical task-evoked data). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This article reports an empirical human fMRI study using a visual alcohol cue reactivity task and reports within-subject contrasts (Alcohol > Control) at the first level and group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses (cluster FWE-corrected results with MNI coordinates). Methods include MRI field strength (3T), preprocessing/statistical software (SPM12), and participant demographics. The paper therefore meets inclusion criteria I3 (visual drug-cue fMRI), I4 (within-participant cue>control contrasts), I5 (group-level voxelwise whole-brain task-evoked results reported), I6 (results reported in main text/figures/tables), and I7 (key methodological/participant details reported). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

The full text reports an empirical fMRI study using visual alcohol-associated cues in abstinent alcohol-dependent patients and matched controls. Methods include a within-participant contrast of alcohol-associated versus control (neutral and scrambled) stimuli at the first level and subsequent group-level random-effects voxelwise analyses. Group results were reported with small-volume correction (volume-of-interest correction) for striatum, ACC and mPFC and coordinates/tables are provided. Participant age/sex, cue type, MRI field strength (1.5T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM99) are reported. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for fMRI visual cue-reactivity and provides qualifying voxelwise task-evoked results suitable for the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study using visual smoking cues with a within-subject smoking>neutral contrast and reports participant demographics, cue type, scanner field strength, and preprocessing software (satisfies I3, I4, I7). However, the paper’s primary analyses extract average beta values from a priori ROIs (4mm spheres) and use these ROI values in Cox/logistic regressions; the manuscript does not report a group-level voxelwise whole-brain or small-volume-corrected task-evoked statistical result (I5 not met). No qualifying voxelwise results are provided in the main text, tables, figures, or supplements to meet I6. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E3 (ROI-only results) and must be excluded. Full text appears complete.

The study is an empirical BOLD fMRI investigation of smoking (drug) cue reactivity using visual stimuli and a validated visual cue task. It reports a within-participant CUE>neutral contrast (abstinence vs. satiety; CUE>neutral) and conducts group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses with multiple-comparison correction (results for ACC reported whole-brain corrected and cluster-corrected). Methods report MRI field strength (3T), preprocessing and statistical software (FSL), participant age/sex, and cue type. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and does not meet any exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-participant cue>control contrast, and is empirical).

This is an fMRI study of smoking cue-reactivity using visual smoking-related pictures versus neutral pictures, with within-participant (smoke>neutral) contrasts for both ‘crave’ and ‘resist’ conditions. Group-level voxelwise analyses were performed using FSL FEAT/FLAME with cluster correction (Z>2.3, cluster p=0.05) and results are reported in tables and figures (coordinates provided). Full text includes introduction, methods (participants, cues, fMRI acquisition, preprocessing, statistical thresholds), results, and discussion. Therefore the study satisfies inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7 and does not meet any exclusion criteria (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-state-only, contains qualifying within-subject cue>control contrasts).

This is an event-related fMRI study of heroin (drug) cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (images). It reports within-subjects Heroin>Neutral contrasts and voxelwise group-level whole-brain analyses (random-effects two-sample t-tests) with FDR correction and coordinates reported. Methods (3T scanner, SPM8, preprocessing, task design) and results (whole-brain activations and coordinate reporting) are fully described. No exclusion criteria are met.

The full text describes a BOLD fMRI study presenting visual marijuana-related cues vs matched non-drug visual cues in treatment-seeking, marijuana-dependent subjects. The paper reports within-subject contrasts (MJ cue > Non-MJ cue) at the group level and provides voxelwise results within an a priori ROI mask that were cluster-corrected via Monte Carlo simulation (i.e., small-volume-corrected). Coordinates are reported in tables and figures; participant demographics, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM2) are described. Thus the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. Full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete.

This is an empirical perfusion fMRI study of smoking (drug) cue reactivity using audiovisual (visual) stimuli. It reports within-participant contrasts of smoking cues vs nonsmoking control cues at the group level with voxelwise statistical maps (t values, cluster-level results), including tables of coordinates and figures. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, enabling assessment. Thus it meets inclusion criteria for visual cue fMRI cue-reactivity analyses and does not meet any exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical task-evoked fMRI study of natural reward (food) cue reactivity using visual stimuli (images). It includes within-participant contrasts of high-calorie (reward-related) > low-calorie (control) food images. Group-level voxelwise results are reported: whole-brain FDR-corrected maps for high>low food cues and small-volume-corrected voxelwise regression analyses within a striatum mask (FDR SVC), with stereotaxic coordinates and figures/tables. Participant demographics, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM12, MATLAB) are reported. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes within-participant cue>control contrasts). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and is suitable for the meta-analysis of visual cue-reactivity for natural rewards.

This full-text fMRI study meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria: it used validated cigarette-related visual cue videos (visual stimuli) (I3); reported within-participant contrasts comparing cigarette cues vs neutral control (crave-allow and crave-resist vs neutral) (I4); performed and reported group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses with cluster correction (FLAME/FEAT, z-thresholds and cluster P-values) and tables/figures of coordinates (I5,I6); and it provides key methodological details including participant demographics, MRI field strength (1.5T), and preprocessing/statistical software (FSL/FEAT) (I7). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion (fulltext_complete). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity- or resting-state-only, includes within-subject cue>control contrasts, and is empirical). Therefore I recommend inclusion.

This is an empirical fMRI study using visual cue-reactivity (video cues) in heroin-dependent and control subjects. It includes within-participant contrasts of heroin cues vs neutral cues (A2 vs A1) and reports group-level voxelwise factorial interaction results with cluster correction and Talairach coordinates (tables and figures). Participant demographics, scanner field strength (1.5T), preprocessing (AFNI), and analysis details are provided. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study using visual smoking videos as cues (I3). It reports within-subject contrasts of smoking>control videos (I4). Group-level voxelwise task-evoked statistical results are reported with multiple-comparisons correction (whole-brain corrected and a priori small-volume correction for DLPFC) and coordinate tables/figures (I5, I6). Participant demographics (age/sex), MRI field strength (1.5T), preprocessing/statistical software (fmristat), and cue type are reported (I7). The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion and appears complete. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes qualifying within-participant cue>control contrasts, and is empirical). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and should be INCLUDED.

The study is an empirical fMRI paper of alcohol cue-reactivity using a multimodal (gustatory + visual label) cue paradigm, includes within-subject Alcohol>Water contrasts, and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results (cluster-corrected Z-statistics) with coordinates in tables. Participant demographics, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (FSL) are reported. The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Thus it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis objective.

This is an empirical fMRI study of cannabis cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (full-color cannabis images) with within-subject contrasts of cannabis images > neutral/control images. The paper reports group-level voxelwise task-evoked results, including small-volume-corrected ROI analyses (Z>2.3, cluster P<0.05 adjusted for small search volumes) and whole-brain cluster-corrected results, with activation clusters localized and reported (tables/figures). Participant demographics, cue type, 3T MRI field strength, and preprocessing/statistical software (FSL/FEAT) are provided. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study of natural reward (appetitive food) cue-reactivity using visual stimuli. It includes a within-participant contrast of food>scrambled control stimuli, and reports group-level voxelwise results: whole-sample whole-brain one-sample t-test and group comparisons within an a-priori ROI with FDR correction (small-volume-corrected voxelwise results). Participant demographics, MRI field strength (3T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM5) are reported. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only; includes qualifying voxelwise task-evoked results). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7.

The full text describes an empirical fMRI study using visual smoking videos (clear visual cue component) with a within-subject design comparing smoking versus neutral videos. The paper reports group-level voxelwise task-evoked results (whole-brain cluster-corrected P < 0.05) with MNI coordinates and tables/figures, and describes methods (subjects, fMRI, analysis with FSL 4.1). Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. The provided full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion and appears complete.

This is an fMRI cue-reactivity study that used visual stimuli (pictures) for gambling (natural reward) and smoking (drug) cues and included within-subject contrasts (gambling>neutral; smoking>neutral). Group-level voxelwise statistical results are reported with cluster-wise family-wise error correction and coordinate information; figures and tables of activations are described. Methods report MRI field strength (3.0T), preprocessing (SPM2) and participant demographics (all-male, Ns), satisfying reporting preferences. Full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, or absence of within-subject cue>control contrasts) are met. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.

Exclusion criteria met: E3 (study reports only ROI-based analyses with no qualifying whole-brain or small-volume-corrected group-level voxelwise task-evoked results). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (task is fMRI of drug cue-reactivity with clear visual smoking-related picture cues), I4 (within-participant smoke>rest contrasts and PSC (smoke–rest) analyses are reported), I7 (participant age range/sex stratification, cue type, MRI field strength (3 T), and preprocessing/statistical software (SPM8/TBV) are reported). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (no group-level whole-brain or small-volume-corrected voxelwise task-evoked statistical results are reported in the manuscript), I6 (not applicable because no qualifying voxelwise results are provided in text, tables, or figures). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore the paper must be excluded for the meta-analysis because it provides only ROI-based task results and lacks the required group-level voxelwise statistical maps or small-volume-corrected results (E3).

This is an empirical fMRI study of natural reward (food) cue-reactivity using visual food images. It includes within-participant contrasts of food cues versus control (HC–C, LC–C, HC–LC) and reports group-level voxelwise whole-brain random-effects analyses (SPM8) with cluster/voxel thresholding and reported activation clusters. Stimuli, MRI field strength (3.0T), preprocessing, and software are described. The full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for inclusion as a whole-brain task-evoked visual cue-reactivity study.

This is an empirical fMRI study of alcohol cue-reactivity using visual stimuli (450-s videos of craving-inducing and aversion-inducing alcohol scenes). The design includes within-participant contrasts (CIC vs mosaic control; AIC vs mosaic control) and group-level random-effects voxelwise GLM analyses producing SPMs with voxelwise FDR correction. Results are reported as whole-brain voxelwise group contrasts with statistics (p-values, FDR thresholds) and regional activations in the main text. MRI field strength (1.5T), preprocessing and analysis software (BrainVoyager), participant demographics and cue types are reported. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore the study meets the review’s inclusion criteria for visual cue fMRI studies with qualifying voxelwise task-evoked results and is suitable for inclusion.

The study is an empirical task-based fMRI experiment with visual reward cues (MID task) and reports within-subject contrasts of reward anticipation (gain cues > ¥0). Group-level voxelwise results are reported (whole-brain analyses and an a priori NAc ROI with FWE small-volume correction), and voxelwise results are presented in text/tables/figures. Participant/method details (age range, task cue types, MRI field strength, preprocessing software) are reported. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, I6, and I7. No exclusion criteria apply. Full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (complete).

This is an fMRI study of natural reward-related visual cue-reactivity (food images). It reports within-participant contrasts comparing high-caloric > low-caloric food (Tea and Water conditions) and interaction contrasts.
